messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir, a 40-year-old software engineer, sat in the therapist's office with an anxious energy that seemed to vibrate through the air. He had come to seek help after months of feeling trapped in his own mind. The traumatic event that had turned his life upside down was a devastating earthquake that struck his hometown, leaving destruction in its wake and claiming lives indiscriminately. Amir vividly recalled that day; the ground shook violently, and buildings crumbled around him. He could still hear the terrifying sounds of metal bending and glass shattering, filling his ears with echoes of chaos. It was an experience that replayed in his mind, a loop of images and sounds that he could not escape.

In the months following the earthquake, Amir struggled to make sense of his new reality. He had always prided himself on being the positive one in his family, the one who could find a silver lining in any situation. Yet, this disaster felt insurmountable. He found himself forcing positive thoughts, trying to convince himself that the future held promise. However, every time he attempted to uplift his spirits, a wave of despair would crash over him, leaving him feeling more isolated and miserable. He was haunted by the sense that he had let his family down; they relied on his optimism, and he felt he was failing them.

The memories of that fateful day intruded on his life, uninvited and relentless. When he closed his eyes, he could hear the haunting sounds—the cries of people trapped beneath rubble, the sirens wailing in the distance. These auditory memories would surface unexpectedly, and he often found himself frozen in fear, as if he were right back in that moment. Confusion plagued him, too; he struggled to put the sequence of events in order, a jumble of sights and sounds that left him disoriented and anxious. Each memory felt vividly real, flooding his senses with visceral reminders of the terror he had experienced.

As time went on, Amir noticed he was increasingly on edge. In meetings at work, he would jump at the slightest unexpected movement, his heart racing as if he were still running for his life. He became hyper-vigilant, always scanning the room for an escape route, his mind fixated on the idea that danger lurked around every corner. This heightened state of alertness led to strained interactions with colleagues, who began to notice his withdrawn demeanor. Amir felt guilty; he was aware that his behavior was affecting his work relationships, yet he couldn’t shake the underlying fear that had taken hold of him.

Amir also developed an aversion to anything remotely related to medical situations. The mere sight of an ambulance or a hospital triggered panic within him, memories of the frantic rush to save lives during the aftermath of the earthquake flooding back with alarming intensity. He would avoid any medical appointments, rationalizing that he was simply too busy at work or too focused on family obligations. This avoidance, however, accumulated over time, leading to a growing sense of neglect regarding his own health.

The weight of his negative appraisals grew unbearable. Amir often found himself reflecting on how he could have avoided the disaster. He believed he should have been more vigilant, more prepared, and that someone else would have handled the situation better. This self-comparison left him feeling trapped in a cycle of shame and guilt. He no longer saw a future that held joy, convinced that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The laughter he once shared with his wife felt distant, as if it belonged to someone else. His happiness had been replaced by a persistent cloud of misery that hung over him.

It was this accumulation of distress that finally pushed Amir to seek help. On a particularly difficult day, after a confrontation with his wife about his withdrawal and moodiness, he felt an overwhelming sense of hopelessness. He realized he could no longer continue living in this state of fear and sadness. In his mind, he clung to the hope that maybe, just maybe, therapy could help him reclaim the happiness he had lost. Yet, beneath that hope lay a deep fear—fear that he would always be trapped in this cycle of pain, unable to escape the memories that haunted him. Amir sat in the office, a mix of apprehension and hope swirling within him, yearning for a way to find peace once more.
